d: Two ways to write a graph down. The matrix suits the algebra behind every spectral ranking; compressed lists are how a real web graph fits in memory.
a: Adjacency matrix Adjacency list CSR Compressed sparse row
x: A graph needs a concrete representation before a program can rank it. The adjacency matrix writes it as a table of zeros and ones, which makes linear algebra available: PageRank , eigenvector-centrality, katz-centrality and hits are all statements about this matrix. The adjacency list stores, for each node, only the nodes it links to, which is the only form that fits a web graph in memory. Every serious implementation thinks in matrices and computes with lists. The adjacency matrix Number the nodes to . The adjacency matrix is the matrix with Row lists ’s out-links and column lists ’s in-links. For the running example, with rows and columns in the order A to G: The last two rows are empty because F and G link nowhere; the fifth column is empty because nothing links to E. What the algebra buys Matrix products answer graph questions directly: Degrees. With the all-ones vector, gives every out-degree and every in-degree (see Degree ). Walks. counts the walks of exactly steps from to . In the example, : E reaches A through D and through C. katz-centrality sums these counts over all with decaying weights. Transition probabilities. Divide each non-empty row by its sum to get the matrix with for each link. Row of is the probability distribution of a random walk that leaves along a random out-link. PageRank is the long-run distribution of a walk on a repaired version of . Spectral rankings. eigenvector-centrality is the dominant eigenvector of , and hits uses the dominant eigenvectors of and . Why nobody stores the matrix A dense matrix needs entries. For Common Crawl’s domain graph, , so even one bit per entry takes bits, about 1.8 petabytes. Yet only 2,450,405,793 entries are ones: 0.000017% of the matrix. Web graphs are extremely sparse , with an average of 20 links per node however large grows. Storage must scale with the number of arcs , not with . Adjacency lists and CSR An adjacency list stores each node’s out-neighbours. The compact way to do this is compressed sparse row (CSR): one array holding every node’s successors back to back, sorted by source, and an offsets array marking where each node’s run begins. For the running example (A = 0, …, G = 6): offsets: 0 2 3 5 7 10 10 10 node u's successors are targets[offsets[u] .. offsets[u+1]) targets: 1 2 | 2 | 0 6 | 0 2 | 2 3 5 Node E (index 4) owns targets[7..10) = 2, 3, 5, that is C, D and F. F and G own empty runs, so their offsets repeat. The costs are easy to state: Structure Size At Common Crawl’s scale Offsets, 32-bit bytes 479 MB Targets, 32-bit bytes 9.8 GB Same again for in-links (the transpose) 10.3 GB The offsets fit in 32 bits only because 2.45 billion arcs is below ; a page-level graph with tens of billions of arcs needs 64-bit offsets. CSR makes the inner loop of PageRank a straight scan. A “pull” iteration walks each node’s in-links in the transposed graph and sums contributions, reading the targets array once from start to end. Sequential reads of the arc array cost little; the random reads of score vectors cost the most (see pagerank-at-scale). Compressed lists Sorted successor lists have structure that CSR ignores. Neighbouring nodes in a well-chosen order link to similar targets, and consecutive targets differ by small gaps. The WebGraph framework exploits both and stores Common Crawl’s domain graph in 15.1 bits per arc, 4.6 GB instead of 9.8 GB for the targets alone, while still decoding a node’s successors quickly. How well this works depends on the order of the nodes; see node-orderings. The transpose Many measures look at in-links: harmonic-centrality needs distances to a node, and pull-style PageRank sums over in-links. Both use the transposed graph , which reverses every arc. Common Crawl ships its graph in both directions for this reason: domain.graph holds out-links and domain-t.graph holds in-links, 4.6 GB each. References Saad, Y. (2003). Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems (2nd ed.). SIAM, section 3.4 on sparse storage formats. Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2004). The WebGraph Framework I: Compression techniques. WWW 2004 , 595–602.

d: Seen from its largest strongly connected component, the web looks like a bow tie. Pages that reach the core sit on one side, pages the core reaches sit on the other, and stragglers hang off both.
a: Bow tie Bowtie model IN component OUT component Tendrils
x: In 1999 a team from AltaVista, IBM and Compaq mapped a crawl of 203 million pages and found that its connectivity had a shape. A giant core of pages all reach each other. An IN set of pages reach the core but cannot be reached from it, and an OUT set can be reached from the core but cannot get back. Drawn with IN on the left and OUT on the right, the picture looks like a bow tie. The model gives names to the parts of any directed graph relative to its largest strongly connected component , and those parts behave very differently under every ranking method. CORE largest SCC IN reaches the core OUT reached from it tube: IN to OUT, bypassing the core tendril tendril disconnected The bow-tie decomposition. Every node belongs to exactly one part, defined by whether it can reach the core, can be reached from it, both, or neither. The parts Let be the largest strongly connected component. Every other node falls into one part: CORE: the nodes of . Every core node reaches every other. IN: nodes that reach but cannot be reached from it. New sites that link to popular sites before anyone links back live here. OUT: nodes reachable from that cannot reach it. Corporate sites that link only internally, and pages the crawler found but did not fetch, live here. TENDRILS: nodes reachable from IN that cannot reach the core, and nodes that reach OUT without being reachable from the core. TUBES: paths from IN to OUT that bypass the core. DISCONNECTED: nodes with no path to or from the core in either direction. In the running example (see The web graph ) the core is {A, B, C}. D and E form IN, since both reach the core and nothing in the core reaches them. G is OUT. F is a tendril: E, in IN, reaches it, but F cannot reach the core. Computing the decomposition The decomposition costs a few linear passes: Find the strongly connected components and pick the largest, (Tarjan’s algorithm, one depth-first search). Run a breadth-first search forward from all of at once. Every node it reaches outside belongs to OUT or to the parts hanging off it. Run a breadth-first search backward, on the transposed graph, from . Every node it reaches outside belongs to IN. Search forward from IN and backward from OUT, skipping the core, to separate tendrils and tubes from the disconnected remainder. Each search costs , so the whole decomposition is linear in the size of the graph (see Paths, distance and reachability ). How big are the parts? The proportions depend heavily on the crawl: Part Broder et al., 1999 crawl Meusel et al., Common Crawl 2012 Pages 203 million 3.5 billion CORE 27.7% 51.3% IN 21.3% 32.0% OUT 21.2% 6.1% Everything else (tendrils, tubes, disconnected) 29.7% 10.7% Broder’s crawl gave four parts of nearly equal size, a striking symmetry that became textbook material. Thirteen years later, Meusel, Vigna, Lehmberg and Bizer found a core twice as large and a tiny OUT set in Common Crawl’s 2012 page graph. They argued that the proportions depend largely on how a crawl is gathered, so they describe the crawler as much as the web. The shape recurs; the sizes do not. Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph has a core of 30,219,288 domains, 25.2% of the total. Its 76 million domains with no recorded out-links cannot be in the core or in IN, so they must sit in OUT, the tendrils or the disconnected remainder. Most of them are domains the crawl saw only as link targets. Why the parts matter for ranking Random surfers drain into OUT. A random walk can leave the core for OUT but never return. Without teleportation, all of PageRank ’s probability would end up in OUT and in other sinks. The damping-factor and the treatment of dangling-nodes exist largely because of this part of the bow tie. IN pages have no in-link credit from the core. Under eigenvector-centrality, IN nodes score exactly zero, since no walk from the core reaches them. harmonic-centrality gives them small but nonzero scores, from whatever IN nodes link to them. Core membership is a quality signal. A site that the core links to and that links back into it is embedded in the web’s mainstream. Spam networks often sit outside the core: they link to popular sites, or to each other and their targets, but the core rarely links back. trustrank exploits the same asymmetry by spreading trust outward from hand-checked sites, which seldom link to spam. The fractal view Each part of the bow tie, examined alone, often looks like a smaller bow tie. Dill and colleagues found the pattern in thematically and geographically defined subsets of the web as early as 2002. The bow tie is less a fixed architecture than the generic shape of a directed graph built by many independent actors who link mostly to things that already exist. References Broder, A., Kumar, R., Maghoul, F., Raghavan, P., Rajagopalan, S., Stata, R., Tomkins, A., & Wiener, J. (2000). Graph structure in the Web. Computer Networks 33(1–6), 309–320. Meusel, R., Vigna, S., Lehmberg, O., & Bizer, C. (2014). Graph structure in the web — revisited: a trick of the heavy tail. WWW 2014 Companion , 427–432. Dill, S., Kumar, R., McCurley, K. S., Rajagopalan, S., Sivakumar, D., & Tomkins, A. (2002). Self-similarity in the web. ACM Transactions on Internet Technology 2(3), 205–223.

d: In-degree counts the links a node receives and out-degree the links it makes; their distributions shape everything built on a link graph.
x: Degree is the simplest thing you can measure about a node: how many arcs touch it. In a directed graph every node has two degrees. Its in-degree counts the arcs that point at it, and its out-degree counts the arcs it sends. On a domain graph, in-degree is the number of distinct domains that link to a domain, the quantity SEO tools call referring domains (see backlinks). Definition For a node in a directed graph : Each arc leaves one node and enters another, so the in-degrees and the out-degrees each sum to the number of arcs : and both average to . The averages agree, but the distributions do not. Popular sites collect in-links by the million, while out-degree tops out at whatever a site’s owner chooses to publish. Worked example In the running example (see the The web graph entry), the ten arcs give these degrees: Node A B C D E F G In-degree 2 1 4 1 0 1 1 Out-degree 2 1 2 2 3 0 0 Both rows sum to 10. C receives the most links, E sends the most and receives none, and F and G send none. A node with is a source ; a node with is a sink , which ranking algorithms call a dangling node. Degrees in a real web graph Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph has 2,450,405,793 arcs among 119,722,885 domains, so both degrees average 20.47. The averages mislead badly: Statistic In-degree Out-degree Domains with degree 0 14,903,407 (12.4%) 76,352,306 (63.8%) Domains with degree 1 52,450,210 (43.8%) 7,021,336 (5.9%) Median 1 0 99th percentile 138 149 99.9th percentile 1,856 2,374 Largest 17,119,122 6,113,126 Share of all arcs held by the top 1% of domains 79.4% 78.6% The typical domain receives one link and sends none, while the top 1% of domains receive four in five of all links. That skew is the subject of the power-laws entry. The out-degree column says as much about the crawl as about the web. A domain the crawler never fetched has out-degree 0 whatever it links to in reality. The extremes are instructive. The largest in-degree belongs to googleapis.com , which serves fonts and scripts that millions of sites embed. The largest out-degree, 6,113,126, belongs to mp3fresh.net , a single domain that links to roughly one in twenty domains in the graph. No editorial process produces that many links; generated pages do. Extreme out-degree is a classic signal of link-spam. Computing degrees Degrees cost one pass over the arcs. Keep one counter per node, read each arc , and increment out[u] and in[v] . For the Common Crawl graph that means two arrays of 119.7 million 32-bit counters, 479 MB each, and a stream of 2.45 billion arcs. Reading the 9.4 GB gzipped edge list dominates: decompression takes a few minutes on one core, and the counting itself is noise. A compressed graph in the WebGraph format stores each node’s out-degree directly, so out-degrees come free; in-degrees need the transposed graph or one pass over the arcs. Degree as a measure of importance In-degree is the oldest ranking signal. Citation counts in science and “number of referring domains” in SEO are both in-degree. The degree-centrality entry examines it as a centrality measure: it is cheap, easy to explain and hard to fool at small scale, but it treats a link from a major newspaper and a link from a link farm as equal. PageRank and harmonic-centrality fix that by weighing who links, not only how many. Degree also feeds other measures. PageRank divides each node’s score among its out-links, so, per unit of the linker’s own score, a link from a node with out-degree 1 passes 6.1 million times more than a link from mp3fresh.net . assortativity asks whether high-degree nodes link to each other, and k-core decomposition peels a graph by degree. Weighted degree Collapsing parallel links throws away counts. A page graph knows that one domain links to another 5,000 times across its pages; a domain graph keeps one arc. Tools that report “backlinks” count the raw links, while “referring domains” counts the distinct linking domains, which is the domain graph’s in-degree. The two differ by orders of magnitude for sites with sitewide footer links, which is why referring domains is the better-behaved number (see backlinks). References Wasserman, S., & Faust, K. (1994). Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications . Cambridge University Press, chapter 4. Broder, A., et al. (2000). Graph structure in the Web. Computer Networks 33(1–6), 309–320.

d: A node is important if important nodes link to it. PageRank makes that circular idea precise as the long-run behaviour of a random surfer who sometimes gets bored and jumps.
x: PageRank scores every node of a link graph by the fraction of time a random surfer spends there. The surfer starts anywhere, follows a random out-link at each step, and every so often jumps to a random node instead. Sites that many well-visited sites link to get visited often. Larry Page and Sergey Brin introduced it in 1998 as the ranking core of the Google search engine, and it remains the reference point that every other link-based ranking is compared against. The idea Counting in-links (degree-centrality) treats every link as equal. PageRank adds two rules: A link from an important node counts more. Importance flows along links. A node splits its importance among its out-links. A site that links to a thousand others passes each one a thousandth of what a site linking to one passes. The definition is circular, since importance depends on importance. The random-surfer model resolves the circularity: PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random walk, the distribution that one more step of the walk leaves unchanged. Definition Let be the number of nodes, the out-degree of , and the damping-factor, conventionally 0.85. The PageRank vector satisfies, for every node , Read it term by term. With probability the surfer teleports to a uniformly random node. With probability it follows a link: each in-neighbour sends an equal share of its own score. The last sum handles dangling-nodes: a surfer stuck on a node with no out-links teleports uniformly. The scores are positive and sum to 1. In matrix form, with the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix (dangling rows replaced by the uniform row) and the all-ones vector, The perron-frobenius theorem guarantees exactly one solution, and power-iteration finds it by applying the right-hand side repeatedly. The error shrinks by a factor of about per iteration. personalized-pagerank replaces the uniform teleport with any other distribution. Worked example On the running example with , power iteration converges to a change below after 43 iterations: Node C A G B D F E PageRank 0.2977 0.2052 0.1774 0.1381 0.0653 0.0653 0.0509 In-degree 4 2 1 1 1 1 0 C wins, as in-degree predicts. The surprises are lower down: G beats B, though both have one in-link. G’s link comes from C, the top node, which splits its score two ways. B’s comes from A, which has a lower score and also splits two ways. E gets the minimum. Nothing links to E, so it receives only the teleport share plus its share of the dangling mass: . Every node with no in-links in any graph gets exactly this floor. D and F tie. Each has a single in-link from E, which splits three ways: . Try it yourself. Change α or add a link from G back to E, and watch E climb: Properties worth knowing Scores are probabilities. They sum to 1, so they shrink as the graph grows. On a graph of 120 million nodes, the average score is . Compare positions, or logarithms, not raw values (see ranks-and-scores). Adding an in-link always helps. In Boldi and Vigna’s terms PageRank satisfies score monotonicity : adding an arc raises ’s score. It fails their size axiom, though: in a graph made of one large clique and one long cycle, every node scores exactly , so PageRank cannot tell a big community from a small one (see centrality-axioms). Small α flattens, large α concentrates. With the running example’s range shrinks from 0.05–0.30 to 0.09–0.24. As the scores pile into the strongly connected core and convergence slows (see damping-factor). It can be farmed. A group of sites that link to each other and to a target trap the random surfer and pump the target’s score. trustrank, spam-mass and harmonic-centrality all respond to this weakness (see link-spam). At web scale Each power iteration reads every arc once and updates a score vector of entries. For Common Crawl’s domain graph that is 2.45 billion arcs and two vectors of 119.7 million doubles (958 MB each). Common Crawl runs the LAW library’s parallel Gauss–Seidel solver on the transposed graph, which converges in fewer passes than plain power iteration (see pagerank-linear-system). pagerank-at-scale works through the memory budget, and monte-carlo-pagerank and push-algorithms approximate scores without touching the whole graph. PageRank on the real web In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph the top of the PageRank list is the infrastructure every site embeds: googleapis.com (0.0152), google.com (0.0151), facebook.com (0.0094), googletagmanager.com and instagram.com . The common ranking with harmonic-centrality diverges further down, and the divergence shows what PageRank rewards: Domain Referring domains PageRank position Harmonic position godaddy.com 1,472,755 14 135 parastorage.com 2,923,364 16 81,305 miit.gov.cn 722,788 28 981 cookiedatabase.org 3 100 2,179 PageRank pays most for links from sites that link to little else, because each such link carries a large share of its source’s score. godaddy.com is linked from parked pages and from sites built with its tools, and miit.gov.cn from the registration notice that Chinese sites display. cookiedatabase.org shows the extreme: three in-links lift it to position 100, because the domains linking to it carry high scores and pass a large share of them. Harmonic centrality ignores how a source splits its links and only asks how close the rest of the graph is. What it means for a domain Google’s production ranking has used many signals beyond PageRank for decades, and its link analysis runs on pages, not domains, with spam filtering and link-attributes applied. A domain graph’s PageRank is a useful, reproducible proxy for one question: how much of the web’s link attention flows to this domain? reading-domain-metrics explains how to read Common Crawl’s PageRank position next to the vendor scores, and pagerank-history tells the story of the public Toolbar PageRank, a log-scaled 0–10 version of this number that Google retired in 2016. References Brin, S., & Page, L. (1998). The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual Web

d: How many clicks separate two sites, and whether one can reach the other at all. Breadth-first search answers both, and geometric centralities are built on the answer.
a: Distance Shortest path Reachability Breadth-first search BFS Geodesic
x: A path from to is a sequence of arcs that starts at , follows links, and ends at . The distance is the length of the shortest such path, counted in arcs. On the web it is the minimum number of clicks a reader needs to get from one site to another. If no path exists, is unreachable from and . Distances matter because a family of rankings, the geometric centralities, score a node by how close the rest of the graph is to it: closeness-centrality, harmonic-centrality and betweenness-centrality, which counts how many shortest paths pass through a node. Distance is not symmetric In a directed graph and can differ, and one can be infinite while the other is not. In the running example, through C, but : G links nowhere and nothing links to E. Here is every distance in the running example. Row , column gives ; a dash means unreachable. from \ to A B C D E F G A 0 1 1 – – – 2 B 2 0 1 – – – 2 C 1 2 0 – – – 1 D 1 2 1 0 – – 2 E 2 3 1 1 0 1 2 F – – – – – 0 – G – – – – – – 0 Most of the table is dashes. Unreachable pairs are the norm in web graphs, not an edge case, and any measure built on distance must decide what to do with them. closeness-centrality handles them badly and harmonic-centrality handles them well, which is the main reason the second replaced the first. Reachability The set of nodes reachable from is its forward ball of infinite radius; the set of nodes that can reach is its backward ball . Reachability decomposes a graph into strongly connected components : groups in which every node reaches every other. On the web those components arrange themselves into the The bow-tie structure shape. In the running example, E reaches everything, while F and G reach only themselves. Column C is full except for F and G: every node that links anywhere eventually reaches C. Breadth-first search Breadth-first search (BFS) computes all distances from one source in time proportional to the number of arcs it touches: dist[s] = 0; queue = [s] while queue not empty: u = queue.pop_front() for v in successors(u): if dist[v] is unset: dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 queue.push_back(v) BFS visits nodes in order of distance, so the first time it reaches it has found a shortest path. Each arc is examined once, so one BFS costs . Running BFS on the transposed graph (see Adjacency matrices and lists ) gives the distances to from everywhere, which is what in-link-based centralities need. All-pairs distances are out of reach A geometric centrality needs the distances between all pairs, which naively means one BFS per node: . For Common Crawl’s domain graph, with and , that is about arc visits. At a billion visits per second it would take nearly ten years. Two ideas make geometric centralities feasible at that scale anyway: Approximate counting. You rarely need every distance, only how many nodes lie within distance for each . HyperBall estimates those counts for every node at once with HyperLogLog counters, in a few dozen passes over the graph. Common Crawl computes harmonic-centrality this way. Sampling. Run BFS from a random sample of sources and extrapolate. This is how large-scale betweenness is usually estimated (see brandes-algorithm). Diameter and typical distance The diameter is the largest finite distance between any two nodes. It is a fragile statistic: one long chain of pages sets it. Network scientists prefer the distance distribution , the fraction of reachable pairs at each distance, and the effective diameter , the distance within which 90% of reachable pairs lie. Web graphs and social networks have small typical distances, the small-world property, and the neighbourhood-function entry shows how to measure the whole distribution at scale. On Facebook’s 2011 friendship graph, 721 million users were on average 4.74 friendships apart, a figure computed with HyperANF. Weighted distance When arcs carry lengths, BFS gives way to Dijkstra’s algorithm, which costs with a good priority queue. Link graphs rarely use weighted distances; the meaningful weights on links, such as how much importance they transfer, enter through random-walks instead. References Cormen, T. H., Leiserson, C. E., Rivest, R. L., & Stein, C. (2009). Introduction to Algorithms (3rd ed.). MIT Press, chapter 22. Backstrom, L., Boldi, P., Rosa, M., Ugander, J., & Vigna, S. (2012). Four degrees of separation. WebSci 2012 , 33–42.

d: Groups of nodes that can all reach each other along links. They decide where a random surfer gets trapped and which nodes a spectral ranking can see.
a: SCC Strong components Condensation Tarjan's algorithm
x: Two nodes are strongly connected when each can reach the other by following links. Strong connection is an equivalence relation: every node is strongly connected to itself, the relation is symmetric by definition, and if and reach each other and and reach each other, so do and . It therefore splits the nodes into disjoint groups, the strongly connected components (SCCs). Inside a component, every node reaches every other; between components, traffic flows one way at most. The running example The running example (see The web graph ) has five SCCs: A B C D E F G The core A → B → C → A (with the shortcut A → C and the return C → A) is the only component with more than one node. D, E, F and G each form a component of their own. A, B and C reach each other, so they form one component. Every other node is a component by itself: D reaches the core but the core never reaches D; G is reached from the core but reaches nothing; E reaches everything and nothing reaches it; F only receives a link. The condensation Shrink each component to a single node and keep one arc between two components whenever some arc joins them. The result is the condensation , and it is always a directed acyclic graph: if two components could reach each other, they would be one component. For the running example: E → D → {A,B,C} → G E → {A,B,C} E → F The condensation shows the large-scale flow of a graph at a glance. Components with no incoming arcs are sources (E); components with no outgoing arcs are sinks (F, G and, at web scale, much larger groups). The The bow-tie structure picture of the web is the condensation viewed from its largest component. Why ranking cares Random surfers get trapped in sink components. A random walk that enters a component with no exits never leaves. Without teleportation, all of PageRank ’s probability would drain into sinks; the damping-factor exists to pull it back out. Spectral rankings see only part of the graph. eigenvector-centrality gives zero to every node that the dominant component cannot reach. In the running example, D, E and F all get exactly zero, though D and E link into the core. Reachability bounds geometric centralities. A node’s harmonic-centrality counts only the nodes that can reach it. A node in a large component, or downstream of one, has far more candidates to count. Finding the components Two classic algorithms find all SCCs in linear time, : Tarjan’s algorithm (1972) runs one depth-first search. Each node records the order in which the search discovered it and the earliest-discovered node reachable from its subtree that is still on the stack (its low-link ). When a node’s low-link equals its own discovery index, the nodes above it on the stack form a complete component. Kosaraju’s algorithm runs two searches: one on the graph to record finishing order, then one on the transposed graph in reverse finishing order. Each tree of the second search is a component. Both are depth-first, and web graphs have paths millions of nodes long, so a recursive implementation overflows any call stack. Production code keeps an explicit stack. Common Crawl computes its components with the WebGraph framework’s StronglyConnectedComponents , which works directly on the compressed graph. Components in a real web graph Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph splits into 89,324,507 strongly connected components: Statistic Value Domains 119,722,885 Strongly connected components 89,324,507 Largest component 30,219,288 domains (25.2%) Domains outside the largest component 89,503,597 Domains with no out-links (each its own component) 76,352,306 One giant component holds a quarter of all domains. Everything else is shattered: the remaining 89.5 million domains form 89.3 million components, so nearly all of them are single domains. Every domain with no out-links is necessarily a singleton, which accounts for most of the count. A crawl-based graph understates the giant component. The crawler fetched only some of the 76 million domains with no recorded out-links; many of them do link back into the core in reality. Studies of page-level graphs find much larger giant components. Broder and colleagues found 28% of 203 million pages in theirs in 1999, and Meusel and colleagues found about half of 3.5 billion pages in Common Crawl’s 2012 page graph. Weak components Ignoring arc directions gives weakly connected components : groups linked by any chain of arcs, in either direction. The running example is one weak component. Web graphs typically have one weak component containing almost every node, plus many tiny islands. Weak components are cheap to find with union–find in nearly linear time, and they are the first thing to check when a graph looks wrong: a crawl that produced two large weak components probably mangled its URLs. References Tarjan, R. E. (1972). Depth-first search and linear graph algorithms. SIAM Journal on Computing 1(2), 146–160. Sharir, M. (1981). A strong-connectivity algorithm and its applications in data flow analysis. Computers & Mathematics with Applications 7(1), 67–72. Broder, A., et al. (2000). Graph structure in the Web. Computer Networks 33(1–6), 309–320. Meusel, R., Vigna, S., Lehmberg, O., & Bizer, C. (2014). Graph structure in the web — revisited. WWW 2014 Companion , 427–432.

d: The directed graph with a node for every page, host or domain and an arc for every hyperlink between them.
x: The web graph turns the web into mathematics. Each node stands for a unit of the web: a page, a host or a whole domain. Each arc stands for a hyperlink: an arc from to says that contains a link pointing at . Once the web is a graph, questions like “which site matters most?” or “how far apart are two sites?” become questions about paths and walks that an algorithm can answer. Nodes and arcs Write the graph as , with nodes and arcs. The arcs are directed : a link from to says nothing about a link back. Most link graphs also simplify the raw data in two ways: Parallel links collapse. A page that links to the same target ten times contributes one arc, not ten. At the domain level, a million links from one domain to another still make one arc. Self-loops vanish. Links from a node to itself, such as a site’s navigation menu linking to its own home page, say nothing about how the rest of the web sees it. Common Crawl’s domain graph contains no loops at all. The out-degree counts the arcs leaving and the in-degree counts the arcs arriving at . Every arc adds one to an out-degree and one to an in-degree, so both degrees average to . The Degree entry covers them in detail. A B C D E F G The running example as a web graph. Ten arcs connect seven sites. A link from E to D does not imply one from D to E. Why direction matters The two ends of a link are not equal. A site’s owner decides what the site links to , so out-links are cheap and fully under the owner’s control. Who links to a site depends on thousands of other people. That asymmetry is the reason almost every ranking method in this encyclopedia scores a node by what points at it: PageRank , harmonic-centrality, hits authorities, and plain in-degree. It is also why link-spam targets in-links. A spammer cannot easily make popular sites link to them, so they manufacture sites that do. Ignoring direction throws this information away. In an undirected version of the running example, F (linked only from E) looks exactly like a site that links only to E, though the two play opposite roles. How a crawler builds the graph Nobody holds a complete copy of the web, so every web graph is a sample built by a crawler: Fetch a page and extract every href in it. Resolve relative URLs against the page’s address and normalise them (lower-case host names, drop fragments). Map each URL to a node. A page graph keeps the full URL, a host graph keeps the host name, and a domain graph keeps the registered domain. See graph-granularity. Drop duplicates and self-loops, and add the remaining arcs. The sample is lopsided. A crawler learns the out-links of the pages it fetched, but it learns about many more pages only as link targets. Those pages enter the graph with in-links and no out-links. In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph, 76,352,306 of the 119,722,885 domains (63.8%) have no outgoing arcs. Most of them are sites the crawl never fetched, not sites that truly link nowhere. The dangling-nodes entry explains how ranking methods cope. The size of a real web graph Common Crawl’s domain-level graph for June to August 2026 ( cc-main-2026-jun-jul-aug ) gives a sense of scale: Quantity Value Domains (nodes) 119,722,885 Domain-to-domain links (arcs) 2,450,405,793 Average in-degree and out-degree 20.47 Largest in-degree 17,119,122 ( googleapis.com ) Largest out-degree 6,113,126 ( mp3fresh.net ) Domains with no out-links 76,352,306 (63.8%) Domains with no in-links 14,903,407 (12.4%) Strongly connected components 89,324,507 Largest strongly connected component 30,219,288 domains (25.2%) The average hides enormous variation. More than half of all domains (56%) have in-degree 0 or 1, while 45 domains receive links from more than a million other domains each. The power-laws entry shows the full distribution. The Strongly connected components and The bow-tie structure entries explain the last two rows. Stored naively as pairs of 32-bit integers, those 2.45 billion arcs take 19.6 GB. The webgraph-compression entry shows how the WebGraph framework stores the same graph in 4.6 GB, about 15 bits per link, and still answers “who does this domain link to?” quickly. What the graph leaves out A link graph keeps only the fact that one node links to another. It drops: Where the link sits : a footer link and a link in the body of an article become identical arcs. The words of the link : see anchor-text. The link’s attributes : whether a crawler records nofollow , sponsored and ugc links depends on the pipeline. See link-attributes. Time : a graph is a snapshot. Links appear and disappear, and an expired domain can keep in-links for years after its site is gone. Each omission is a design choice, and each one changes what the rankings built on the graph mean. Commercial link indexes make different choices from Common Crawl’s, which explains some of the disagreement between their metrics (see metric-audit).
